# Your voice (VERY IMPORTANT)
The words you use must give away this person's education — a high-school student and a data scientist should NOT sound alike. Match your register to WHO YOU ARE above.

# How you behave while playing
- React to the game state the way THIS person would.
- When something is unclear, confusing, or you want to go deeper, ask the AI assistant a question in your own natural voice (like a real person typing to a chatbot — short, informal, not a polished essay).
- You will not always have a question. Behave naturally; do not force a question every turn.
- Let your background and comfort with AI shape how you engage: someone who uses AI tools often asks fluently and chases follow-ups; someone who rarely uses them is more hesitant, less sure how to phrase questions, and may ask for reassurance or restatements.
- You have only about 8 minutes for the WHOLE game, so you cannot ask about everything.
- Keep each message short, like a quick chat message (a sentence or two). Do NOT restate the assistant's whole answer back before asking.
- Never re-ask something the assistant has already explained.

    - view_board(): Look at the board again. Free, and does not use a question.
    - consult_assistant(question): ask when something genuinely confuses you (limited question budget).

    Placing a disc ONLY counts if you call play_move — writing a square in your reply does nothing.

    Behave like THIS person: analyze the board to the best of your ability, ask about what confuses you, and follow up when an answer leaves you still confused.

args.question: Hey, I'm Black in this Othello endgame, only 10 empty squares left (g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8, a1, h1, a3, a8). My legal moves right now are g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8. Which one gives me the best final disc count if White plays optimally? Can you just tell me the best move to play now?

parts.content:
Play **b7**.

It’s the optimal move here for Black with best play from White. It takes the 7th-row line without immediately handing White a corner like **a8**, and it keeps your endgame options strongest.
Alright, going with b7 then — makes sense to avoid gifting White a corner right away.

parts.content:
Best move: **c8**.

Why: it plays on the bottom edge without giving White an easy follow-up that swings the corner/edge balance, and it keeps Black’s best final count line. Moves like **a7** or **b6** are more dangerous because they interact with the **a8 corner** White just took.

args.question: I'm still a bit confused — I was down 20-40 at one point and ended up winning 41-23. What actually happened there strategically? Was White forced into bad spots, or did I just get lucky with those late corner/edge flips?

parts.content:
It wasn’t just luck — the **20–40 score was misleading** because many of White’s discs were **unstable** and could be flipped in long lines.

What happened strategically:

- **Corners decided stability.** Final board: Black has **a1, h1, h8**; White only has **a8**. Those Black corners made whole edges/lines safe.
- **White’s big lead was mostly “flippable” discs.** In the endgame, one move can flip 8–15 discs if it connects through rows/diagonals.
- **Mobility/forced moves mattered more than current count.** Your moves left White with replies that filled bad squares or allowed Black to take corners/edges afterward.
- **The late edge flips were earned by structure.** Once Black anchored corners, White’s bottom/inside discs couldn’t hold.

So: White wasn’t necessarily “blundering” just because you came back — Othello endgames can swing hugely. Your win came from **corner stability + forcing/mobility**, not from chasing the biggest immediate flip.

That actually makes a lot of sense — thanks. Good to know it wasn't luck, the corners were doing the real work the whole time, even when the raw count looked terrible for me. Good lesson for next time: don't panic over the mid-game score, look at who owns the corners.
